newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FOCUS-Israeli finance chief quits, lending rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Israeli finance chief quits, lending rate cut.

text.p: Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor quit on Wednesday in a tiff with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over currency reforms adopted by the cabinet.
The changes, approved overnight despite opposition by the finance chief, prompted the Bank of Israel to lower its key lending rate by 1.2 percentage points, the first reduction since February.

Israeli shares closed higher in the heaviest trading in three years in response to the rate cut, with the market shrugging off the power struggle between Meridor and Netanyahu that went beyond their dispute over the reforms.
Meridor, citing Netanyahu's "ulterior motives", handed in a letter of resignation after ministers at a seven-hour special cabinet decided to widen the exchange rate band of the shekel.
"There was no reason to bring this issue (to the cabinet) today," a bitter-sounding Meridor, Netanyahu's long-time rival in the ruling Likud party, told a news conference.

"When it became clear to me that there were ulterior motives for this whole affair, I informed the ministers and the prime minister that I intend to resign from the government," adding the trading band question could have been dealt with in budget discussions due to be held in another two months.
Meridor strongly opposed widening the shekel's trading bands, fearing it would lead to a further appreciation of the Israeli currency, hurt exports and cause the economy to slow.
He hinted the row over how far the shekel should be allowed to fluctuate against a basket of foreign currencies was the ammunition Netanyahu needed to squeeze him out.
"Netanyahu's sudden interest in the trading band...was a little strange," he said at the news conference.
Netanyahu went on the offensive after the resignation, telling Israeli radio and television stations in a series of interviews that Meridor had rejected compromises.

"I don't know why there was a reason to adopt such a harsh position when far-reaching compromises were made with the finance minister and I don't understand the need to resign and the need to make groundless and false accusations," Netanyahu told Israel Radio.

Netanyahu said he intended to appoint a new finance minister "quickly". Analysts speculated Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon, who led Israel's settlement drive in the occupied West Bank as housing minister from 1988 to 1992, was the leading candidate.
Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, warned that markets would be nervous with a Sharon appointment for fear the populist ex-general would not maintain budgetary restraint.
The shekel has been allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency by six percent a year.
But high interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the Bank of Israel to buy massive amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band.

Under the new plan, adopted in the cabinet by a vote of eight to three, the lower band remains the same while the upper band rises to 21 percent. The spread between the top and bottom band was therefore extended to 28 percent.
The central bank hopes the move will eliminate the need for contant interventions in the currency market.
Economists and market analysts generally praised the economic measures but said they would produce no dramatic changes in the exchange rate or economic growth.
Netanyahu only reluctantly appointed Meridor, widely regarded to be on the Likud's moderate wing, to be finance chief a year ago under pressure from party activists.
Netanyahu narrowly escaped indictment recently in a government corruption scandal over the short-lived appointment of an attorney-general.
The prime minister was widely reported to have been angered by what he considered Meridor's lukewarm support while Netanyahu was battling influence peddling allegations since January.
